But if someone says: Can you not say that they share in the quality of being most unjust? That is, this is the most unjust thing, and that is the most unjust thing?

We say: That is not possible, because you cannot pair one who prevents the mosques of Allah from having His name mentioned in them with one who fabricates a lie against Allah. Which of the two is greater?

The second. So they cannot share in being most unjust, and then the first meaning is determined. What is the first meaning?

That the superlative is relative to the meaning for which it was brought, or in which it was brought: ﴿Who is more unjust than one who fabricates a lie against Allah?﴾

Commentary of Ibn 'Uthaymin (Tafsir al-Quran al-Karim) on surah 18, verse 16:

﴿And when you have withdrawn from them and from what they worship other than Allah, then retreat to the cave﴾ [Al-Kahf: 16]. Who is the speaker of this? The speaker is the youths (al-fityah). That is, some of them said to others: since you have withdrawn from your people and from what they worship besides Allah, that is, their idols, ﴿then retreat to the cave﴾, meaning, take refuge in the cave. The definite article (al) in ﴿the cave﴾ may be for specific reference (al-'ahd), as if it were a cave they were accustomed to retreating to; or it may be for perfection (al-kamal), meaning the perfect cave that will protect you from your people. As for the first, it requires evidence, meaning that it is for specific reference, and we would need to know that these youths used to go to a particular cave in which they took refuge.

As for the second, its basis is that they were seeking only a cave that would shelter and protect them, so the article (al) is for denoting perfection; i.e., retreat to a cave that will shelter you and protect you from your enemy.

﴿Your Lord will spread out for you of His mercy and will prepare for you of your affair a means of ease (mirfaqan)﴾; meaning, if you do that, Allah the Exalted will make the matter easy for you, because whoever leaves something for the sake of Allah, Allah compensates him with something better.

Here is a question: His saying ﴿then retreat to the cave﴾ — the particle "fa" (then) suggests to the mind that it is the answer of a condition (shart), and it is well known that "idh" (when) is not a conditional particle; the conditional particle is "idha" (if/when), or "idh" when it is joined with "ma". But if it is not joined with "ma", is it not conditional?

The answer to this may be given as follows: either it has been given the meaning of a condition, so the answer comes as ﴿then retreat to the cave﴾; or the "fa" is for division (al-tafriq), not for linking, and the meaning is: then, at that time, when you have withdrawn from them, retreat to the cave.

As for His saying ﴿and will prepare for you of your affair a means of ease (mirfaqan)﴾, i.e., He will prepare for you of your situation.

﴿Mirfaqan﴾, i.e., a place by which you may be comfortable (turtafiqun bihi).

And you see the sun, when it rises, inclining away from their cave to the right. (Qur'an 18:17) Here the Almighty says: "And you see the sun when it rises..." — O man, you see the sun when it rises.

"...inclining away from their cave to the right." Regarding the word ﴿تَزَاوَرُ﴾ (tazāwaru) there are two readings: ﴿تَزَّاوَرُ﴾ (tazzāwaru), whose original form is tatazāwaru, and ﴿تَزَاوَرُ﴾ (tazāwaru) with the lighter pronunciation. The meaning is that it inclines.

"...from their cave to the right." Imagine how the cave would be now. If the sun inclines away from it to the right, then the entrance of the cave faces north. For this reason some said: the mouth of the cave faces Banat Na'sh (Banāt Naʿsh, the "Daughters of the Bier"), which are well-known stars in the sky that people of the desert know.

"And when it sets, it passes them on the left." It is on the left side of the cave.

Regarding the word ﴿تَقْرِضُهُمْ﴾ (taqriḍuhum): it was said the meaning is "it leaves them," and it was said the meaning is "it touches them." The closer view is that it touches them. The benefit of this contact is so that their bodies are protected from change, because the sun, as people say, is a source of health and benefit for a human being.

"...passing them on the left, while they are in a spacious place from it." The pronoun in ﴿وَهُمْ فِي فَجْوَةٍ مِنْهُ﴾ (wahum fī fajwatin minhu) refers to these youths. This fajwa means the inner space; that is, they are not directly beside the doorway, but in an inner place, because that is better for their protection.

In His saying, "When it rises, it inclines [away from them]" and "When it sets, it passes them," there is evidence that the sun is what moves, and by its movement occur sunrise and sunset. This is contrary to what people say now, that the earth is what revolves and the sun is stationary. We have in the words of Allah something that we must take in its apparent sense, and not depart from this apparent sense except by clear evidence. If it is established for us by decisive proof that the alternation of night and day is due to the earth's rotation, then the verses must be interpreted to match reality, and we say: "when it rises" according to appearance, "when it sets" according to appearance, "inclines" according to appearance, (taqriḍ) according to appearance. But before it is made clear to us by decisive proof that the sun is stationary and the earth is what revolves, and by its revolution night and day alternate, we do not accept this at all. We must say that the sun is what, by its movement, produces night and day, because Allah attributed the actions to it, and when the sun set, the Prophet (ﷺ) said to Abu Dharr: "Do you know where it goes?" and he attributed the going to it. We know with certainty that Allah, the Exalted, is most knowing of His creation, and we do not accept innovation or conjecture. But if we were certain that the sun is fixed in a place and the earth revolves, and the alternation of night and day is thereby explained, then interpreting the verses becomes obligatory so that they do not contradict a definitively established matter.

Allah, the Exalted, says: ﴿That is among the signs of Allah﴾. The pronoun in ﴿That﴾ refers to what? To the state of these youths: their leaving their people, their seeking refuge in this cave, and Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, facilitating for them a cave that is perfectly suitable. There is no doubt that this is among the signs of Allah that point to His wisdom and His mercy, the Mighty and Majestic. Should we consider this a karāma (a miracle granted to a righteous person)? The answer: yes, we consider it a karāma without doubt.

﴿Whomever Allah guides is the guided one, and whomever He leaves astray, you will never find for him a guiding ally.﴾ O Allah, guide us and protect us from misguidance.

﴿Whomever Allah guides﴾: this ﴿man﴾ is conditional, and the evidence that it is conditional is the deletion of the yāʾ from yahdi. The response is ﴿then he is the guided one﴾.

Regarding ﴿fahuwa al-muhtad﴾: its original form is al-muhtadī with a yāʾ, but the yāʾ was deleted for lightness, as it was deleted in His saying: ﴿al-Kabīr al-Mutaʿāl﴾ [Ar-Ra'd 9].

﴿And whomever He leaves astray﴾ means: whom He decrees to be astray.

﴿you will never find for him a guiding ally﴾ means: one who would take charge of him and guide him to what is right. In this statement from Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, there is a reminder that we ask for guidance only from Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, and that we do not despair when we see someone who is astray, because misguidance is in whose hand?

In the hand of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic. So we believe in al-qadar (divine decree), and we do not resent the misguidance that occurs from Allah. But it is obligatory upon us to guide these misguided people. Here there is a legislated command and a decree: as for the decree, it is obligatory for you to be content with it in every situation; and as for what is decreed, it has detail: what is legislated, it is obligatory for you to be content with it in every situation. So we are content in that Allah, the Exalted, made people into two categories: guided and astray. But along with that, it is obligatory upon us to strive for the guidance of creation.

Allah the Exalted says: ﴿And you would think them awake, while they were asleep﴾ [al-Kahf 18:18]. ﴿You would think them﴾ means the one who sees them, that is, O beholder, when you see them you would think they are awake, because there are no signs of sleep on them. A sleeper is relaxed and his eyes are closed, but these appear as though they are awake. That is why a person can distinguish between a sleeping man and a man lying down from the moment he sees him. Even if the one lying down tried to feign sleep to deceive his companion, he would be recognized as not asleep. So when you see them, you would think them awake, which indicates that their bodies remained fresh and strong and did not change.

﴿While they were asleep﴾: plural of (rāqid), meaning sleeping.

﴿And We turned them to the right and to the left﴾. This is from the wisdom of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic. That is, at one time they lie on their right side, and at another time on their left. Allah did not mention the back or the belly, because sleeping on the right or the left is the most complete (manner of sleep).

His saying ﴿We turn them﴾ contains evidence that the actions of a sleeper are not attributed to him. What is the basis of this inference? Allah attributed their turning to Himself. So if a sleeping person says in his sleep, "My wife is divorced," would she be divorced?

*Students: No.

*The Shaykh: If he says in his sleep, "I owe so-and-so a thousand riyals," is it established? No, because he has no intention and no will, neither in speech nor in action.

As for the wisdom of turning them to the right and to the left, some scholars said: so that the earth would not consume the side that is in contact with it. But the correct view is that this is not the wisdom. The wisdom is for the balance of blood in the body, so that they remain balanced, because the blood circulates through the body. If it stayed on one side, the upper side would be in danger of being deprived of it. But Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, in His wisdom, made them turn over.

﴿And We turned them to the right and to the left, while their dog was stretching forth his forelegs at the threshold﴾. That is, the dog, as if, and Allah knows best, did not sleep.

﴿Stretching forth his forelegs﴾: that is, sitting on his belly with his forelegs extended.

﴿At the threshold﴾. What is the (waṣīd)? Al-waṣīd is the opening of the cave or the courtyard of the cave. That is, either he is at the opening, or he is beside the cave in its courtyard to guard them. In this there is evidence for the permissibility of keeping a dog for guarding, guarding of humans. As for guarding livestock, the Sunnah has come with it, and guarding crops has come with it in the Sunnah. Guarding a human is more deserving of permission, because if it is permissible to keep a dog to guard livestock or for hunting, which is an enhancement and not a necessity, then keeping it to guard the house is more deserving.

Allah the Mighty and Majestic said: ﴿If you had looked at them, you would have turned away from them in flight, and you would have been filled with dread of them﴾. ﴿If you had looked at them﴾, O beholder, upon them, ﴿you would have turned away from them in flight﴾: awe that Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, places in the heart of whoever sees them, so that no one attempts to approach them. Therefore He said, ﴿you would have turned away from them in flight﴾, even though they did not pursue him, but he is frightened of them.

﴿And you would have been filled with dread of them﴾. (Mulli'ta): his heart would be filled entirely with terror. This indicates the intensity of the fear that befalls whoever sees them.

Commentary of Ibn 'Uthaymin (Tafsir al-Quran al-Karim) on surah 18, verse 19:

Allah the Exalted said: ﴿And thus We roused them, that they might question one another.﴾ [Al-Kahf 19] That is: just as We did for them, by this care in making the cave easy for them, and by letting them sleep this long period, Allah roused them. In other words, We did a similar deed: We did another act for them.

﴿That they might question one another.﴾ As is the customary practice, when people sleep they ask one another when they awake. Some of them say: "What did you see in your dream?" and some say: "Perhaps your sleep was pleasant," and similar things. ﴿One of them said: "How long have you stayed?"﴾ As is the usual custom: how long have we been sleeping?

﴿They said: "We have stayed a day or part of a day."﴾ ﴿We have stayed a day﴾ means: a full day.

﴿Or part of a day﴾ means: part of the day. This is because they had entered at the beginning of the day and were roused from sleep at the end of the day, so they said: "We have stayed a day," if this was the second day, "or part of a day," if this was the first day. This indicates the depth of their sleep.

﴿They said: "We have stayed a day or part of a day."﴾ ﴿They said﴾ means: some of them said to others.

﴿Your Lord knows best how long you have stayed.﴾ It seems these speakers felt that the sleep had been long, but they could not determine it precisely. As for the first speakers, they determined it based on what? Based on the apparent evidence. And as for the others, they did not determine it, based on reality, because a person distinguishes between brief sleep and lengthy sleep. Then some of them said to others: ﴿So send one of you with this silver coin of yours to the city﴾. Send him with your silver; al-Warq is silver, as in the hadith: «And in silver (al-riqah) is one-fortieth.» They had dirhams of silver. ﴿So send one of you with this silver of yours to the city, and let him see which is the purest food, and bring you provision from it.﴾ This includes, firstly: the permissibility of appointing an agent (tawkil) in buying, from their saying: ﴿So send one of you﴾, and appointing an agent in buying is permissible, and in selling is permissible too. It is not hidden that the Messenger (ﷺ) appointed one of his companions to buy a sacrifice for him; he gave him a dinar and said: «Buy a sacrifice», and he bought two sheep with the dinar, then sold one of them for a dinar, so he returned with a sheep and a dinar. The Prophet (ﷺ) then prayed for him that Allah bless his trade, and he would not buy dust without profiting from it.

The scholars have derived from this hadith that the action of the unauthorized agent (tasarruf al-fuduli) is permissible; that is, it is permissible for a person to dispose of another's property if he knows that the other would be content with that. These people appointed one of them to go to the city and bring provision. This also indicates that there is no harm in a person seeking the best food, from their saying: ﴿let him see which is the purest food﴾.

It also contains evidence against the view of the jurists that it is not valid to describe with the superlative form (al-af'al). Do you understand this? Good. The description with the superlative means: it is not permissible to say: "I sell it to you as the best wheat there is." They said: this is not permissible, because there is no good thing except that something better is above it. But it is said that this returns to custom; so "best" means in that time and in that place. ﴿Let him see which is the purest food﴾. Is there any Sunnah that testifies to seeking the purest food?

The answer: Yes. The Prophet (ﷺ) approved of the Companions who exchanged inferior dates for good dates so that the Prophet (ﷺ) might eat from them, and he did not forbid them from this; he did not say: "This is extravagance, so leave off seeking the best." A person has been granted latitude by Allah to choose the best of food or drink, or dwellings, or clothing, or mounts, so long as Allah has given him the ability to do so; he is not blamed.

﴿And let him bring you provision from it﴾ means: he buys and brings it to them. Thus in the appointment of the agent they combined buying and bringing.

﴿And let him be discreet and let no one become aware of you.﴾ ﴿And let him be discreet﴾ means: let him deal secretly, lest they become aware of them and they be harmed. This means that they thought they had stayed only a little while.

﴿And let no one become aware of you﴾ means: let him not make anyone aware of you. Then they gave a reason for this command with the discretion and the prohibition of making them known.

Commentary of Ibn 'Uthaymin (Tafsir al-Quran al-Karim) on surah 18, verse 20:

﴿Indeed, if they gain the upper hand over you, they will stone you or force you back into their religion, and then you will never succeed.﴾ [al-Kahf: 20] Meaning: if you return to their religion ﴿ever﴾; meaning that they will certainly kill you or turn you back on your heels after your faith. In this is evidence for taking precaution against enemies by every means, except forbidden means, for those are forbidden and a person may not fall into them.

And thus We caused them to be discovered" (﴿وَكَذَلِكَ أَعْثَرْنَا عَلَيْهِمْ﴾). He said: add to their resurrection that Allah caused them to be discovered, meaning He let their people come upon them.

﴿That they might know that the promise of Allah is true and that the Hour is not to be doubted﴾. Allah let their people come upon them "so that they might know that the promise of Allah is true." Why?

There are two possibilities. Either the meaning is the establishment of the Hour, which these people denied, or it is that Allah the Exalted saves the believers from the disbelievers, because these seven youths were saved from a great nation that fought them and forbade them from tawhid (monotheism). The apparent meaning is that they might know that the promise of Allah is true in granting victory to His allies.

﴿And that the Hour is not to be doubted﴾. "The Hour" means the establishment of the Hour. "Not to be doubted" means there is no doubt about it; it is an event that will certainly occur.

Then He the Exalted said: ﴿when they disputed among themselves about their affair﴾, connected to ﴿We caused them to be discovered﴾. We caused them to be discovered until they disputed among themselves about their affair. Who are the ones disputing?

* The students: Their people.

* The Shaykh: Their people disputed among themselves. What shall we do with them? Shall we leave them, or what shall we do?

﴿And they said, "Build over them a structure."﴾ Is the meaning: build over their graves, so that the wall is over the grave, or is the meaning: enclose them with it? The second is what is intended: build around them a structure so that it becomes a sign among the signs.

﴿Their Lord is most knowing of them﴾. That is, they hesitated over their affair: how could they remain three hundred and nine years without eating, drinking, or even changing? ﴿Their Lord is most knowing of them﴾; they paused. ﴿Those who prevailed over their affair said﴾, and they were their rulers, ﴿Those who prevailed over their affair said, "We will surely take over them a place of worship."﴾ That is, around them. They said: instead of building a structure to enclose them and conceal them, so that they would have no trace, they took over them a place of worship, they built the mosque over them. The apparent meaning is that they did this, because who was speaking? The rulers who held the dominance. This act, namely taking mosques over graves, is one of the means of shirk (association of partners with Allah), and our Shari'ah has come to combat it. So much so that the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "May Allah curse the Jews and the Christians; they took the graves of their prophets as places of worship," warning against what they did.[[Agreed upon; al-Bukhari (436) and Muslim (531/22), from the hadith of 'A'isha and Ibn 'Abbas.]]

Commentary of Ibn 'Uthaymin (Tafsir al-Quran al-Karim) on surah 18, verse 22:

Then He, Mighty and Majestic, said: ﴿They will say, "They were three, the fourth of them being their dog," and they will say, "They were five, the sixth of them being their dog," guessing at the unseen; and they will say, "They were seven, and the eighth of them was their dog."﴾ [al-Kahf 22]. Here ﴿They will say, "They were three"﴾ and then "They will say, five." How can there be two statements from one speaker? This is explained in two ways. Either the meaning is: some of them will say, "Three, the fourth of them being their dog," another part will say, "Five, the sixth of them being their dog," and a third part will say, "Seven, and the eighth of them being their dog." Or the meaning is: they will be hesitant about this; sometimes they say three, sometimes they say five, and sometimes they say seven. Both are possible and do not contradict one another; you will find them saying one thing at times and another at other times, according to what comes to their minds.

Allah the Exalted said: ﴿guessing at the unseen﴾. This was said about those who said, ﴿They were three, the fourth of them being their dog﴾ and ﴿They were five, the sixth of them being their dog﴾. Allah, Blessed and Exalted, stated concerning both statements that they said them guessing at the unseen; that is, conjecturing about the unseen, without certainty.

﴿And they will say, "They were seven, and the eighth of them was their dog"﴾. He did not say "guessing at the unseen" about this one; rather He remained silent, may He be glorified and exalted. This indicates that their number is seven, with the eighth being their dog, because when Allah refuted the first two statements and remained silent about the third, the third became the correct one.

A parallel to this is the saying of Allah, Blessed and Exalted, about the polytheists when they committed an indecency: ﴿They say, "We found our fathers doing it, and Allah has commanded us to it."﴾ [al-A'raf 28]. The first is one claim, and the second is another claim. Allah said: ﴿Say, "Indeed, Allah does not command indecency."﴾ He remained silent about their saying, "We found our fathers doing it," and refuted their saying, "Allah has commanded us to it." This indicates that the first is correct.

So we also say: since He said "guessing at the unseen" concerning the first two statements and remained silent about the third, we say: therefore we are certain that they were seven, and the eighth of them was their dog.

Allah, Mighty and Majestic, said: ﴿Say, "My Lord knows best their number; none knows them except a few."﴾ That is: when dispute arises, say to the people, ﴿My Lord knows best their number﴾. Has Allah informed us of this number? Answer me.

* Students: Yes.

* The Shaykh: Yes, He has informed us that they were seven, and the eighth of them was their dog. That is: since Allah knows their number best, it is obligatory for us to return to what Allah has informed us, and to say with certainty that their number was seven, and the eighth of them was their dog. ﴿Say, "My Lord knows best their number; none knows them except a few."﴾ That is: none knew them, before Allah informed us that they were seven and the eighth of them was their dog, except a few.

Then Mighty and Majestic said: ﴿So do not argue concerning them except with an outward argument﴾, that is: concerning their affair, their time, their place, their number, their outcome. ﴿Do not argue concerning them except with an outward argument﴾, that is: except with an outward debate that does not reach the heart; because when debate reaches the heart, the debater becomes agitated and angry, his veins swell, and he is affected. But since debate about them is of little benefit, Allah said: ﴿Do not argue concerning them except with an outward argument﴾, an argument on the tongue that does not reach the what? The heart.

﴿And do not seek a ruling concerning them from any of them﴾, that is, do not seek a ruling about the People of the Cave from anyone among the people, whether from the People of the Book or others, ﴿any of them﴾.

Allah, Mighty and Majestic, said: ﴿Why do they not bring a clear authority concerning them?﴾ What is "authority" in the general sense?

* Student: Everyone who has authority or jurisdiction is an authority (sultan).

* The Shaykh: Authority of what?

* The Student: Everyone who has authority is a sultan.

* The Shaykh: Whether it is in evidence, in power, or otherwise; that is: the ruler is a sultan, a man over his family is a sultan, and so on; proof is a sultan. What is meant by it in this verse?

* Student: Proof.

* The Shaykh: Proof, good.

His saying: ﴿And when you withdraw from them and what they worship, except Allah﴾. The phrase ﴿except Allah﴾ may be an exception from His saying ﴿they worship﴾; in that case these people worship Allah and worship other than Him, and the youths withdrew from them, worshipping none but Allah. It may also be that "except" (illa) is disjunctive, and the meaning is that these people do not worship Allah at all; the meaning of the verse would then be: "when you withdrew from them and what they worship" in general, then He said "except Allah," meaning you did not withdraw from them but rather you believed in Him. It may also be an exception made out of caution; that is, these youths said "and what they worship except Allah," fearing that someone among their people might worship Allah.

His saying: ﴿So retreat to the cave﴾. What is the fa' here?

* Student: It may be that it is in the response of a condition.

* The Shaykh: It may be in the response of a condition; and what about "idh"?

* Student: (...) a condition.

* The Shaykh: Yes indeed. And what else?

* Student: (...) for sequencing.

* The Shaykh: That the fa' is for sequencing, and that "idh" remains as it is, an adverb of time.

His saying: ﴿And you would see the sun when it rises﴾ to the end. What did we take as evidence for what?

* Student: That the sun is what moves.

* The Shaykh: Yes, that the sun is what moves, and the shade and the light are due to the movement of the sun. Should we remain upon this?

* Student: We say: if a definitive proof is established that the sun...

* The Shaykh: No. Should we remain upon this or not? Say: yes or no.

* Student: Yes.

* The Shaykh: Yes, we remain upon this as an obligation, unless it is established by a sensory means that convinces us that the sun is stationary and the earth is what revolves; then we believe in that and say: the Noble Qur'an addressed people according to their observation; that is, according to what they see.

His saying: ﴿and you would have been filled with dread of them﴾. Why did He not say "and fear would have seized you"? Which of them is more emphatic?

* Student: The first.

* The Shaykh: And that is?

* Student: "You would have been filled with dread of them."

* The Shaykh: ﴿You would have been filled with dread of them﴾, because it indicates that they were filled with terror, not only in the heart. Do you understand?

* Student: Yes.

* The Shaykh: Why did Allah, Mighty and Majestic, cast awe upon whoever saw them and looked upon them?

* Student: So that he would not turn toward them.

* The Shaykh: Yes, that is, for their protection. Good, well done.

His saying: ﴿And We raised them up that they might question one another﴾. The lam, which we did not mention: is it the lam of causation or the lam of consequence? It is the lam of consequence; that is, they were not raised for the purpose of questioning, but they were raised and then questioned one another. The lam comes for consequence, as in the saying of Allah: ﴿Then the family of Pharaoh picked him up, that he might become for them an enemy and a grief﴾ [al-Qasas 8]. The lam is not for causation at all, and it cannot be for causation, because the family of Pharaoh did not pick him up for this purpose; rather they picked him up, and so he became for them an enemy and a grief.

Why did they say: ﴿We have remained a day or part of a day﴾?

* Student: (...).

* The Shaykh: Yes; because they slept at the beginning of the day and were raised at its end, so they thought it was part of a day, or a whole day if they had slept the previous day. Is that correct? Good.

Does this story show the permissibility of appointing an agent?

* Student: As they said: ﴿So send one of you with this silver of yours to the city﴾.

* The Shaykh: Yes.

* Student: So they appointed one of them to buy food for them from the city...

* The Shaykh: And bring it.

* Student: Yes, the buying along with bringing it.

* The Shaykh: Good.

Does the verse indicate that there is no harm in a person requesting the better food?

* Student: His saying: ﴿purer food﴾.

* The Shaykh: ﴿Purer food﴾. And has the Sunnah come with this?

* Student: (...).

* The Shaykh: Yes, good; may Allah bless you.

What was the outcome of these youths with regard to their people?

* Student: They disputed concerning them.

* The Shaykh: They disputed concerning them; would they build a structure over them or leave them? And the result, that is, the final thing?

* Student: Those of them who held power, the people of dominance, said: build a mosque over them.

* The Shaykh: ﴿We will surely take over them a place of worship﴾, correct. That is: we will build over them a place that becomes a site of prostration, where people come and prostrate.

What do you say: were they three, five, or seven?

* Student: Seven.

* The Shaykh: Seven. The evidence?

* Student: The verse's preference after hesitation.

* The Shaykh: The verse's preference after hesitation, I did not understand.

* Student: The verse confirmed that they were seven, and the eighth was their dog, after the people had hesitated about their number.

* The Shaykh: No.

* Student: That Allah mentioned the first two statements and refuted them with His saying: ﴿guessing at the unseen﴾.

* The Shaykh: Yes indeed, that Allah mentioned the first two statements, three and five, and refuted them with His saying "guessing at the unseen," and mentioned the third statement and remained silent about it. Good. The refutation of the two and the silence about the third?

* Student: It indicates that it is the correct one.

* The Shaykh: It indicates that it is the correct one. Is there a parallel to this?

* Student: The saying of Allah, Mighty and Majestic: ﴿And when they commit an indecency, they say, "We found our fathers doing it, and Allah has commanded us to it." Say, "Indeed, Allah does not command indecency."﴾ [al-A'raf 28]. Allah refuted their saying, "Allah has commanded us to it," and remained silent about their saying, "We found our fathers doing it."

* The Shaykh: So this indicates that their saying "We found our fathers doing it" is correct, is that right? Good, may Allah bless you.

Allah the Exalted said: ﴿Say, "My Lord knows best their number; none knows them except a few." So do not argue concerning them except with an outward argument﴾. That is: it does not reach the heart; make your argument an outward argument. From this is derived: that one should not weary his heart with debate about a matter in which debate is of no benefit. This happens often: sometimes some people become heated when they are argued with about something in which debate is useless. We say: my brother, do not argue; keep your argument only on the tongue, not reaching the heart, so that you do not become heated and angry. This indicates that whatever has no good in it should not be probed deeply. This is common.

It is found most of all in the science of kalam (theology); the theologians who delved into tawhid and creed bring up things of no benefit, such as their saying: the succession of events in eternity past, in the future, and similar empty talk with no need for it. They write pages in establishing this question, by negation or affirmation, though there is no profit in it. So do not weary yourself with a thing that has no benefit; and if you see your companion engaging in argument, say to him: reflect on the matter and close the door. Some people, may Allah protect us, are infatuated with argument, and no people have been afflicted with argument except that they went astray, and we seek refuge in Allah.

﴿So do not argue concerning them except with an outward argument, and do not seek a ruling concerning them from any of them﴾, that is: do not ask anyone about their condition. * In this there is an indication that a person should not seek a ruling from someone who is not qualified to give rulings, even if he claims to have knowledge; do not seek a ruling from him if he is not qualified.

Commentary of Ibn 'Uthaymin (Tafsir al-Quran al-Karim) on surah 18, verse 23–24:

﴿And never say of anything, "Indeed, I will do that tomorrow," (23) unless [you add], "If Allah wills."﴾ [Al-Kahf: 23, 24] ﴿And never say﴾: the address here is to the Messenger ﷺ, like the address in the verse before it. ﴿And never say of anything﴾, i.e., concerning something, ﴿"Indeed, I will do that tomorrow"﴾. They mentioned[[Narrated by al-Tabari in his Tafsir (15/143) from the hadith of Ibn 'Abbas.]] that the Quraysh sent to the Jews in Medina, and they said: "A man has been raised among us who claims that he is a prophet." The Jews said to them: "Ask him about three things: ask him about the youths who went out from their city and took refuge in a cave, what was their matter? And ask about the man who ruled the eastern and western parts of the earth, and ask him about the soul." Three things. So they asked the Prophet ﷺ about the People of the Cave, and he said: "I will inform you tomorrow." The revelation then paused for about fifteen days, during which no revelation came to him. The Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him and his family, did not know the stories of earlier peoples, as Allah the Exalted says: ﴿And you did not recite before it any book, nor did you write one with your right hand﴾ [Al-'Ankabut: 48]. But Allah the Exalted tested him and examined him, so He withheld the revelation for fifteen days, just as He tested Sulayman, peace be upon him, when he said: "Tonight I will go around to ninety women, each of whom will bear a boy who will fight in the way of Allah." Then the angel said to him: "Say: If Allah wills." He did not say: "If Allah wills." So he went around to the ninety women, having relations with them. And what happened? "One of them bore a half of a human being."[[Agreed upon; al-Bukhari (6639) and Muslim (1654/25) from the hadith of Abu Hurayrah.]] So that Allah the Exalted shows His servants that the matter is His, and that a person, however high his rank with Allah the Exalted and however honored he is, has no escape from the decree of Allah.

The revelation remained withheld for fifteen days. It is well known that the Prophet, peace be upon him, would be afflicted with grief and worry lest these people use the delay in informing them of that as a means to deny him. In truth, this was not a means to deny him. That is, they might say: "Muhammad promised us he would inform us tomorrow, and he did not do so. Where is the revelation he claims is sent down to him?" But we say: the delay of the revelation and the delay of the Prophet ﷺ in informing them of it indicates what? It indicates his truthfulness. For had he been a liar, he would have fabricated a story overnight, fabricated a story and said: "This is their story," so that they would not accuse him. So the delay of the revelation, and the Prophet ﷺ not informing them, indicates his perfect truthfulness ﷺ.

﴿Indeed, I will do that tomorrow (23) unless [you add], "If Allah wills."﴾ Do not say: "Indeed, I will do it," except with a statement joined to the will of Allah. Joining it with the will of Allah benefits a person in two great ways:

The first: that Allah makes the matter easy for him, since he has entrusted it to Him, may He be exalted.

The second: if he was swearing an oath, he does not break it.

* From His saying ﴿Indeed, I will do﴾ it is derived that if he says: "I will do this" as a report, not as a firm assertion that the action will certainly occur, then it does not necessarily require him to add the exception of the will. That is: if your companion says to you: "Will you pass by me tomorrow?" and you say: "Yes," now you have said: "You will pass," but is this a report or is it something that will certainly happen? The answer: this is a report. But if you want to say that it will certainly happen, then say: "If Allah wills." The reason for this: the first is a report about what is in your heart, and what is in your heart exists now; but that you will do it in the future is a report about something that has not yet occurred, and you do not know whether it will occur or not. Pay attention to this difference.

If a person says: "I will travel tomorrow," then if he is reporting what is in his heart, he does not need to say "If Allah wills." Why? Because it is a report about something that is happening. But if by his saying "I will travel" he means that he will undertake the journey and actually travel, then here he must say: "If Allah wills." For this reason the noble verse came: ﴿Indeed, I will do that tomorrow﴾ and did not say "Indeed, I will do," but rather said ﴿Indeed, I will do﴾. So do not say of a future thing that you will do it except joined with the will of Allah.

﴿And remember your Lord when you forget﴾: that is, remember your Lord; i.e., the command of your Lord that you should say "If Allah wills," ﴿when you forget﴾ to say it, because a person may forget. And if he forgets, Allah the Exalted has said: ﴿Our Lord, do not impose blame on us if we forget or make a mistake﴾ [Al-Baqarah: 286]. The Prophet ﷺ also said: "Whoever sleeps through a prayer or forgets it, let him pray it when he remembers it."[[Agreed upon; al-Bukhari (597) and Muslim (684/314), and Abu Ya'la (3086), with his wording, from the hadith of Anas.]] As for the will (of Allah), when a person forgets, when should he say it? When he remembers it. But does it benefit him? That is, if he breaks the oath, is the expiation not obligatory for him, or does it not benefit him?

Some scholars said: it benefits him, even if he remembers only after a day or two, or a year or two; because Allah stated without restriction: ﴿And remember your Lord when you forget﴾.

Other scholars said: it does not benefit him, unless he remembers within a short time, such that the exception is built upon what it is an exception from. This is the view of the majority of scholars.

I will give an example to make the matter clear. If you say: "By Allah, I will certainly do this," and you forget to say "If Allah wills," then you remember ten days later and say "If Allah wills," and then you do not do it, based on the view that whoever says "If Allah wills" does not break the oath: does this benefit him or not?

Some scholars said: it benefits him, because here he said: ﴿And remember your Lord when you forget﴾.

Others said: it does not benefit him, because the speech was not built one part upon another. So what is the benefit of Allah's command that we remember Him when we forget? He said: the benefit is the removal of sin; because Allah said: ﴿And never say of anything, "Indeed, I will do that tomorrow," (23) unless [you add], "If Allah wills."﴾ So if you forget, then say it when you remember. But will it benefit you so that you do not break the oath, or is the sin removed from you by that? The apparent view is the second: that the sin is removed. As for breaking the oath, he breaks it if he violates it, because the exception with respect to breaking the oath does not benefit unless it is connected.

Then, is connection to be understood as the speech being continuous, one part with another, or as long as they remain in the same gathering?

There is also a difference of opinion on this. Some say: as long as they are in the gathering, it is connected; when he rises from the gathering, it has been cut off. They said: because the Prophet ﷺ said: "The two parties to a sale have the option" until what? "As long as they have not separated,"[[Agreed upon; al-Bukhari (2079) and Muslim (1532/47) from the hadith of Hakim ibn Hizam.]] so he made separation a cutoff.

Others said: no, what matters is the continuity of the speech, one part with another. The apparent view, and Allah knows best, is that if he is in his gathering and has not uttered any words that cut off between the two statements, then there is no harm in his making the exception.

﴿And say: "Perhaps my Lord will guide me to something nearer to right guidance than this."﴾ ﴿Perhaps my Lord will guide me﴾: ﴿perhaps (ʿasā)﴾ here carries the meaning of hope when it comes from a created being, and the meaning of certainty when it comes from the Creator. Pay attention: when it comes from a created being, it indicates hope; when it comes from the Creator, it indicates occurrence. So the saying of Allah, blessed and exalted: ﴿Except the oppressed among men, women, and children, who have no ability to devise a way and are not guided to a path. (98) For those, perhaps Allah will pardon them﴾ [An-Nisa: 98, 99], we say: here ʿasā indicates occurrence.

And Allah the Exalted said: ﴿The mosques of Allah are only maintained by those who believe in Allah and the Last Day, establish prayer, give zakah, and fear none but Allah﴾ — then what? ﴿So it is expected that those will be among the guided﴾ [At-Tawbah: 18].

As for when it comes from a human being, it indicates hope. So the saying of His, mighty and majestic: ﴿And say: "Perhaps my Lord will guide me"﴾ indicates hope. ﴿Will guide me my Lord﴾: that is, will direct me to the way. For this reason He said: ﴿to something nearer to right guidance than this﴾. Did He do so or not? He, mighty and majestic, did so. But the Messenger ﷺ, when he first said: "I will inform you tomorrow,"[[Narrated by al-Tabari in his Tafsir (15/143) from the hadith of Ibn 'Abbas.]] needed to wait for the command of Allah, mighty and majestic: ﴿And say: "Perhaps my Lord will guide me to something nearer to right guidance than this."﴾

Commentary of Ibn 'Uthaymin (Tafsir al-Quran al-Karim) on surah 18, verse 23–24:

﴿And never say of anything, "Indeed, I will do that tomorrow," (23) unless [you add], "If Allah wills."﴾ [Al-Kahf: 23, 24] ﴿And never say﴾: the address here is to the Messenger ﷺ, like the address in the verse before it. ﴿And never say of anything﴾, i.e., concerning something, ﴿"Indeed, I will do that tomorrow"﴾. They mentioned[[Narrated by al-Tabari in his Tafsir (15/143) from the hadith of Ibn 'Abbas.]] that the Quraysh sent to the Jews in Medina, and they said: "A man has been raised among us who claims that he is a prophet." The Jews said to them: "Ask him about three things: ask him about the youths who went out from their city and took refuge in a cave, what was their matter? And ask about the man who ruled the eastern and western parts of the earth, and ask him about the soul." Three things. So they asked the Prophet ﷺ about the People of the Cave, and he said: "I will inform you tomorrow." The revelation then paused for about fifteen days, during which no revelation came to him. The Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him and his family, did not know the stories of earlier peoples, as Allah the Exalted says: ﴿And you did not recite before it any book, nor did you write one with your right hand﴾ [Al-'Ankabut: 48]. But Allah the Exalted tested him and examined him, so He withheld the revelation for fifteen days, just as He tested Sulayman, peace be upon him, when he said: "Tonight I will go around to ninety women, each of whom will bear a boy who will fight in the way of Allah." Then the angel said to him: "Say: If Allah wills." He did not say: "If Allah wills." So he went around to the ninety women, having relations with them. And what happened? "One of them bore a half of a human being."[[Agreed upon; al-Bukhari (6639) and Muslim (1654/25) from the hadith of Abu Hurayrah.]] So that Allah the Exalted shows His servants that the matter is His, and that a person, however high his rank with Allah the Exalted and however honored he is, has no escape from the decree of Allah.

The revelation remained withheld for fifteen days. It is well known that the Prophet, peace be upon him, would be afflicted with grief and worry lest these people use the delay in informing them of that as a means to deny him. In truth, this was not a means to deny him. That is, they might say: "Muhammad promised us he would inform us tomorrow, and he did not do so. Where is the revelation he claims is sent down to him?" But we say: the delay of the revelation and the delay of the Prophet ﷺ in informing them of it indicates what? It indicates his truthfulness. For had he been a liar, he would have fabricated a story overnight, fabricated a story and said: "This is their story," so that they would not accuse him. So the delay of the revelation, and the Prophet ﷺ not informing them, indicates his perfect truthfulness ﷺ.

﴿Indeed, I will do that tomorrow (23) unless [you add], "If Allah wills."﴾ Do not say: "Indeed, I will do it," except with a statement joined to the will of Allah. Joining it with the will of Allah benefits a person in two great ways:

The first: that Allah makes the matter easy for him, since he has entrusted it to Him, may He be exalted.

The second: if he was swearing an oath, he does not break it.

* From His saying ﴿Indeed, I will do﴾ it is derived that if he says: "I will do this" as a report, not as a firm assertion that the action will certainly occur, then it does not necessarily require him to add the exception of the will. That is: if your companion says to you: "Will you pass by me tomorrow?" and you say: "Yes," now you have said: "You will pass," but is this a report or is it something that will certainly happen? The answer: this is a report. But if you want to say that it will certainly happen, then say: "If Allah wills." The reason for this: the first is a report about what is in your heart, and what is in your heart exists now; but that you will do it in the future is a report about something that has not yet occurred, and you do not know whether it will occur or not. Pay attention to this difference.

If a person says: "I will travel tomorrow," then if he is reporting what is in his heart, he does not need to say "If Allah wills." Why? Because it is a report about something that is happening. But if by his saying "I will travel" he means that he will undertake the journey and actually travel, then here he must say: "If Allah wills." For this reason the noble verse came: ﴿Indeed, I will do that tomorrow﴾ and did not say "Indeed, I will do," but rather said ﴿Indeed, I will do﴾. So do not say of a future thing that you will do it except joined with the will of Allah.

﴿And remember your Lord when you forget﴾: that is, remember your Lord; i.e., the command of your Lord that you should say "If Allah wills," ﴿when you forget﴾ to say it, because a person may forget. And if he forgets, Allah the Exalted has said: ﴿Our Lord, do not impose blame on us if we forget or make a mistake﴾ [Al-Baqarah: 286]. The Prophet ﷺ also said: "Whoever sleeps through a prayer or forgets it, let him pray it when he remembers it."[[Agreed upon; al-Bukhari (597) and Muslim (684/314), and Abu Ya'la (3086), with his wording, from the hadith of Anas.]] As for the will (of Allah), when a person forgets, when should he say it? When he remembers it. But does it benefit him? That is, if he breaks the oath, is the expiation not obligatory for him, or does it not benefit him?

Some scholars said: it benefits him, even if he remembers only after a day or two, or a year or two; because Allah stated without restriction: ﴿And remember your Lord when you forget﴾.

Other scholars said: it does not benefit him, unless he remembers within a short time, such that the exception is built upon what it is an exception from. This is the view of the majority of scholars.

I will give an example to make the matter clear. If you say: "By Allah, I will certainly do this," and you forget to say "If Allah wills," then you remember ten days later and say "If Allah wills," and then you do not do it, based on the view that whoever says "If Allah wills" does not break the oath: does this benefit him or not?

Some scholars said: it benefits him, because here he said: ﴿And remember your Lord when you forget﴾.

Others said: it does not benefit him, because the speech was not built one part upon another. So what is the benefit of Allah's command that we remember Him when we forget? He said: the benefit is the removal of sin; because Allah said: ﴿And never say of anything, "Indeed, I will do that tomorrow," (23) unless [you add], "If Allah wills."﴾ So if you forget, then say it when you remember. But will it benefit you so that you do not break the oath, or is the sin removed from you by that? The apparent view is the second: that the sin is removed. As for breaking the oath, he breaks it if he violates it, because the exception with respect to breaking the oath does not benefit unless it is connected.

Then, is connection to be understood as the speech being continuous, one part with another, or as long as they remain in the same gathering?

There is also a difference of opinion on this. Some say: as long as they are in the gathering, it is connected; when he rises from the gathering, it has been cut off. They said: because the Prophet ﷺ said: "The two parties to a sale have the option" until what? "As long as they have not separated,"[[Agreed upon; al-Bukhari (2079) and Muslim (1532/47) from the hadith of Hakim ibn Hizam.]] so he made separation a cutoff.

Others said: no, what matters is the continuity of the speech, one part with another. The apparent view, and Allah knows best, is that if he is in his gathering and has not uttered any words that cut off between the two statements, then there is no harm in his making the exception.

﴿And say: "Perhaps my Lord will guide me to something nearer to right guidance than this."﴾ ﴿Perhaps my Lord will guide me﴾: ﴿perhaps (ʿasā)﴾ here carries the meaning of hope when it comes from a created being, and the meaning of certainty when it comes from the Creator. Pay attention: when it comes from a created being, it indicates hope; when it comes from the Creator, it indicates occurrence. So the saying of Allah, blessed and exalted: ﴿Except the oppressed among men, women, and children, who have no ability to devise a way and are not guided to a path. (98) For those, perhaps Allah will pardon them﴾ [An-Nisa: 98, 99], we say: here ʿasā indicates occurrence.

And Allah the Exalted said: ﴿The mosques of Allah are only maintained by those who believe in Allah and the Last Day, establish prayer, give zakah, and fear none but Allah﴾ — then what? ﴿So it is expected that those will be among the guided﴾ [At-Tawbah: 18].

As for when it comes from a human being, it indicates hope. So the saying of His, mighty and majestic: ﴿And say: "Perhaps my Lord will guide me"﴾ indicates hope. ﴿Will guide me my Lord﴾: that is, will direct me to the way. For this reason He said: ﴿to something nearer to right guidance than this﴾. Did He do so or not? He, mighty and majestic, did so. But the Messenger ﷺ, when he first said: "I will inform you tomorrow,"[[Narrated by al-Tabari in his Tafsir (15/143) from the hadith of Ibn 'Abbas.]] needed to wait for the command of Allah, mighty and majestic: ﴿And say: "Perhaps my Lord will guide me to something nearer to right guidance than this."﴾

**Commentary of Ibn 'Uthaymin (Tafsir al-Quran al-Karim) on surah 18, verse 25:**

Allah the Exalted said: ﴿They remained in their cave three hundred years and added nine﴾ [al-Kahf 25]. ﴿They remained﴾ means: these youths.

We mentioned that this divides into?

* Student: Into two types; (...) so he does not need to say "in shaa' Allah." But if he intends to bring the action about, he says "in shaa' Allah."

* Shaykh: Yes. If he is reporting what is in his own mind, he does not need to say "in shaa' Allah," because what is in his mind has already occurred, and Allah the Mighty and Majestic has willed it. For example, if someone is asked, "When will you travel?" and he says, "I will travel tomorrow," he is reporting what is in his mind and what he intends, and there is no need to say "in shaa' Allah." But if he wants to bring the action about and carry it out, he must say "in shaa' Allah."

Can this distinction be understood from the verse?

* Student: Yes, because Allah said ﴿Indeed I am doing﴾ with emphasis.

* Shaykh: ﴿Indeed I am doing﴾, and He did not say "I will do."

* Student: Yes.

* Shaykh: "Doing" (fa'il), as if it were a firm, emphatic statement that "I will do it." This is one aspect. Another aspect: what is in his inner self has already been willed by Allah. If he is reporting what is in his inner self, then Allah has willed it, so there is no need to say "in shaa' Allah," because he is reporting what is in his inner self.

The words of the Exalted: ﴿And remember your Lord when you forget﴾. What is its meaning?

* Student: That is: remember the command of your Lord when you forget, and say "in shaa' Allah."

* Shaykh: Yes. If you forget to say "in shaa' Allah," then remember the command of Allah the Mighty and Majestic, and seek forgiveness for your sin, because you have opposed what Allah commanded. It has also been said that ﴿remember your Lord﴾ means the exception (istithna', the exception clause in speech). Is it valid for the exception to be separated from the thing excepted from?

* Student: There is a difference of opinion on it.

* Shaykh: Yes. What is the difference?

* Student: Some of them said: the exception is valid even if a long time has passed.

* Shaykh: Even after a period of time.

* Student: Even after a period of time.

* Shaykh: That is, if he swore, saying, "By Allah, I will do such-and-such on Friday," and forgot to say "in shaa' Allah," then on Thursday he remembered and said "in shaa' Allah." Does it benefit him or not?

* Student: According to this opinion, it benefits him.

* Shaykh: According to this opinion it benefits him, correct. What is the second opinion?

* Student: The second opinion: it is necessary for the exception to be connected in speech.

* Shaykh: The exception must be connected to the thing excepted from. Good. But does it benefit him?

* Student: It benefits him in that it removes the sin.

* Shaykh: In removing the sin from him, correct. This is the position held by the majority of scholars.

It is related that when the Abbasid caliph al-Mansur heard that Abu Hanifa (may Allah have mercy on him) denied the statement of Ibn 'Abbas that the exception benefits even after a period of time[[Reported by Sa'id ibn Mansur in his tafsir (1333) from Ibn 'Abbas, with the wording: that he used to hold that the exception benefits even after a year.]], and you know that al-Mansur was of the descendants of the family of the Prophet (ﷺ), and Ibn 'Abbas held that the exception benefits in terms of the ruling and removing sin even if a long time passes, he summoned him and said: "How do you oppose Ibn 'Abbas?" He said: "O Commander of the Faithful, this is from your good fortune. Consider: people pledge allegiance to you and swear oaths to you. If we adopt the view of Ibn 'Abbas, and they leave your presence, they will say 'in shaa' Allah,' and when they say 'in shaa' Allah,' the oath they swore to you is void." This was from Abu Hanifa's shrewdness, and he was not reprimanded for it, because if we validated the view of Ibn 'Abbas, then those who pledge allegiance and covenant with Allah, when they leave, would say "in shaa' Allah," and then the pledge would be void. So he (al-Mansur) withdrew; that is, his purpose was that he removed the blame from him and did not punish him.

Allah the Blessed and Exalted said: ﴿They remained in their cave three hundred years and added nine (26). Say: Allah knows best how long they remained﴾ [al-Kahf 25–26], and so on to the end. ﴿They remained﴾ means: the People of the Cave. ﴿In their cave﴾ means: the one they chose for themselves, and slept in.

﴿Three hundred years﴾. ﴿Three hundred﴾ is conventionally written with a ta' marbuta on "thalath" (three) joined to "mi'a" (hundred), and "mi'a" is written with an alif, but this alif is not pronounced. Those whom we often hear saying "thalath ma'a" make a mistake. How can they say "ma'a" when it is "mi'a" in the Noble Qur'an: ﴿They remained in their cave three hundred﴾? Some write "thalath" alone and "mi'a" alone, and this is also correct. In my own copy it is written this way: ﴿thalatha mi'a﴾, with "thalath" alone and "mi'a" alone. This is a sound rule.

As for His words ﴿mi'a sinin﴾, ﴿mi'a﴾ has tanwin (nunation), and ﴿sinin﴾ is an explanatory apposition (atf bayan) to ﴿thalatha mi'a﴾. This is because "three hundred" without the word "sinin" would leave us not knowing whether it means three hundred days, three hundred weeks, or three hundred years. When He said ﴿sinin﴾, He clarified this. Then He says ﴿and added nine﴾, meaning they added nine to the three hundred. So how long was their stay? Three hundred and nine years.

Someone may say: why did He not say "three hundred and nine years"? We say: this has the same meaning, and there is no difference. But the Great Qur'an is the most eloquent speech, and for the harmony of the verses and their endings, He said ﴿three hundred years and added nine﴾. It is not as some have said, that ﴿three hundred years﴾ is by the solar calendar and ﴿added nine﴾ is by the lunar calendar. We cannot bear witness on behalf of Allah that He meant this. Who can testify on Allah that He meant three hundred solar years and nine additional lunar years? Even if you agree that three hundred solar years equal three hundred and nine lunar years, we cannot bear witness on Allah to this, because the reckoning is one. And what are the signs by which reckoning is done with Allah the Mighty and Majestic? The crescent moons. Therefore we say: the view that ﴿three hundred years﴾ is solar and ﴿added nine﴾ means lunar is a weak view. Firstly, we cannot bear witness on Allah that He meant this.

Secondly, the number of months and years with Allah is by the crescents: ﴿It is He who made the sun a shining radiance and the moon a light, and determined for it stations, that you might know the number of years and the reckoning﴾ [Yunus 5].

﴿And added nine﴾. Therefore they remained three hundred and nine years by the lunar reckoning.

"Say: God knows best how long they stayed." ﴿قُلِ اللَّهُ أَعْلَمُ بِمَا لَبِثُوا﴾ ﴿Say﴾: O Muhammad, God knows best how long they stayed. This sentence supports the view of those who say that His words ﴿and they stayed in their cave﴾ are part of the speech of those who discuss how long the People of the Cave remained in their cave, namely the Jews, who claim that the Torah indicates this. Accordingly, on this view, His words ﴿and they stayed﴾ are the object of an omitted verb of saying, and the sense is: they said, "They stayed in their cave three hundred years," and then He said: ﴿Say: God knows best how long they stayed.﴾ However, although some exegetes have said this, the correct view is otherwise. So whose speech is His words ﴿and they stayed﴾?

* Student: It is the speech of God.

* The Shaykh: It is the speech of God, and His words ﴿Say: God knows best how long they stayed﴾ are for emphasis (tawkid), i.e., to affirm the sentence that they stayed in their cave three hundred years. The meaning is: say, "God knows best how long they stayed." And He has told us how long they stayed: three hundred years, and they added nine.

﴿To Him belongs the unseen of the heavens and the earth.﴾ That is, to Him belongs what is hidden in the heavens and the earth, or to Him belongs the knowledge of the unseen of the heavens and the earth, and both meanings are true. (ghayb, the unseen) ﴿The heavens⁠﴾ is the plural of (sama', heaven), and they are seven, as is well known, and the earth likewise is seven earths. No one knows the unseen of the heavens and the earth except God; therefore whoever claims knowledge of the unseen is a liar. The unseen here means the future.

As for the present or the past, whoever claims knowledge of it is not an unbeliever, because such a thing has already occurred and some people know it. But knowledge of the unseen future belongs only to God, the Mighty and Majestic; therefore whoever goes to a soothsayer (kahin), asks him about the future, and believes him, has disbelieved in God the Mighty and Majestic, because he has denied His words: ﴿Say: None in the heavens and the earth knows the unseen except God﴾ [an-Naml 65].

As for what is occurring, it is well known that what is occurring is unseen relative to some people and witnessed relative to others. Now, what is in the street is unseen to us, but witnessed by someone who is there. ﴿To Him belongs the unseen of the heavens and the earth.﴾

﴿See Him well and hear Him well.﴾ The grammarians call this an exclamatory verb (fi'l ta'ajjub): (abṣir) means "how well He sees," and (asmi') means "how well He hears," and it denotes the utmost degree of these two attributes, sight and hearing. God, blessed and exalted, sees everything; He sees the crawling of an ant on a black rock in the darkness of night, and He sees what human eyes cannot perceive, what is more hidden and subtle. Likewise in hearing, He hears everything; He knows the secret and what is more hidden than the secret, and He knows the open speech: ﴿And if you speak aloud, then indeed He knows the secret and what is more hidden﴾ [Ta-Ha 7].

A‘ishah, may God be pleased with her, said regarding the story of the woman who disputed (mujadilah) and whose husband had declared her unlawful (zihar) and who came complaining to the Messenger ﷺ, while A‘ishah was in the room, and the room is small as is well known, and the Messenger ﷺ was conversing with the woman, and some of her speech was hidden from A‘ishah, while God the Mighty and Majestic says: ﴿God has heard the speech of she who disputes with you concerning her husband and complains to God, and God hears your exchange﴾ [al-Mujadilah 1]. She said: "Praise be to God, who has encompassed all voices in His hearing. I was in the room, and some of her speech was hidden from me, yet God the Mighty and Majestic is above everything, and despite that He heard her speech and her conversation with the Messenger ﷺ."[[Narrated by an-Nasa'i (3460) and Ibn Majah (188) from the hadith of A'ishah.]]

Believing that God, may He be exalted, has piercing sight that nothing escapes, and penetrating hearing that nothing eludes, requires a person not to let his Lord see him doing what God dislikes, nor hear him saying what God dislikes. For when you believe that whatever deed you do, He sees you, and whatever word you speak, He hears you, this obliges you to fear God the Mighty and Majestic, and not to do any act God dislikes, nor to say any word God dislikes. But faith is weak, so you find a person, when he wants to say or do something, it does not occur to him that God hears or sees, unless he is reminded. Heedlessness is widespread, so it is incumbent upon all of us to pay attention to this great point.

He said: ﴿They have besides Him no guardian.⁠﴾ ﴿They have﴾: does the pronoun refer to the People of the Cave or to whoever is in the heavens and the earth? The second is the one that is definite; that is, no one has a guardian besides God. Even the disbelievers have God as their Guardian, and even the believers have God as their Guardian. God the Exalted says: ﴿Then when death comes to one of you, Our messengers take him, and they do not neglect. Then they are returned to God, their true Master﴾ [al-An'am 61-62]. So God is the Guardian of everyone; this is the general guardianship (al-wilayah al-'ammah). Does God not provide sustenance for the disbelievers, nourish their bodies, subject to them what is in the heavens and the earth, and subject to them the sun, moon, stars, and rains, and likewise the earth? This is a form of guardianship, and He also takes charge of the believers, but this is general guardianship.

The special guardianship is for the believers. God the Exalted says: ﴿God is the Guardian of those who believe; He brings them out of darkness into light. And those who disbelieve, their guardians are the false deities; they bring them out of light into darkness﴾ [al-Baqarah 257]. Special guardianship entails special care: O God, make us among Your friends. It entails that God the Exalted guides the servant, opening for him the doors of beneficial knowledge and righteous action. Therefore He said: ﴿He brings them out of darkness into light.⁠﴾ With what does He bring them out? With knowledge. He first teaches them, and then brings them out.

Thus ﴿they have﴾ means: the people of the heavens and the earth have; ﴿besides Him﴾ means: other than Him; ﴿no guardian﴾ means: one who manages their affairs and arranges them. As for the grammar of this sentence: ﴿mā﴾ is a negation particle, ﴿lahum﴾ is a predicate preceding its subject, and ﴿min waliyy﴾ is a postponed subject to which the superfluous preposition has been attached. For if you removed (min) and said, "They have besides Him a guardian," the sentence would be sound; but (min) came for emphasis and to make the generality explicit, meaning that there can be no guardian for the people of the heavens and the earth other than God, the Mighty and Majestic.

﴿And He does not share His command with anyone.⁠﴾ He does not make anyone a partner in His command: ﴿The command is only for⁠﴾ whom? ﴿God⁠﴾ [al-An'am 57]; ﴿And whatever you differ over, its judgment is with God﴾ [ash-Shura 10]. Command is both cosmic (kawni) and legislative (shar'i). The creation, determination, and management of these great creatures is cosmic; judgment among people through commands and prohibitions is legislative.

So does His words ﴿and He does not share His command with anyone﴾ refer to both or to one of them? It refers to both: no one shares God, the Mighty and Majestic, in His command, neither the cosmic nor the legislative.

* And in it: evidence for the obligation of returning to God's legislative ruling, and that it is not for us to legislate in the religion of God what is not part of it, neither in acts of worship nor in transactions.

As for those scholars who say that we may legislate in transactions what suits the time, this is a false view, for on their view we would be permitted to allow usury (riba), to allow gambling (maysir), and to allow everything that involves gain even if it is forbidden. There is no doubt that this view is false. The Shari'ah is suitable for every time and place, and the last of this Ummah will not be reformed except by what reformed its first.

Regarding the cosmic command, does anyone share God in it? Never, and no one claims this. Can anyone send down rain? No. Can anyone make the earth grow plants? No. No one claims a share in the cosmic command. The legislative command is the one over which humans differ, and some claim that they may legislate for people whatever they consider suitable.

﴿And recite what has been revealed to you of the Book of your Lord﴾. This is a consequence of His saying: ﴿and He does not make anyone a partner in His command﴾. The word ﴿recite﴾ (ittlu) includes both recitation by the tongue (tilawa lafziyya) and recitation in practice (tilawa 'amaliyya). Recitation by the tongue is obvious; you say, "So-and-so recited Surat al-Fatiha to me." Practical recitation (al-tilawa al-hukmiyya al-'amaliyya) means acting upon the Qur'an. When you act upon it, you have "recited" it, meaning you have followed it. For this reason, we say about His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Indeed, those who recite the Book of Allah and establish prayer﴾ [Fatir 29], that it includes both recitation by the tongue and practical recitation.

As for His saying: ﴿And recite what has been revealed to you of the Book of your Lord﴾ [al-Kahf 27], the address is to the Messenger, may Allah's peace and blessings be upon him. However, know that the address directed to the Messenger ﷺ is divided into three categories:

The first: what the evidence shows is specific to him, so it is specific to him.

The second: what the evidence shows is general, so it is general.

The third: what may bear both meanings. It has been said that it is general, and it has been said that it is specific to him, while the Ummah follows it, not by the force of this address, but by the force of his being their model and exemplar.

An example of the first, where evidence shows it is specific to him, is His saying, Blessed and Exalted is He: ﴿Did We not expand for you your breast?﴾ [al-Sharh 1]. There is no doubt that this is specific to him. And ﴿Did He not find you an orphan and give you shelter?﴾ [al-Duha 6] is specific to him.

An example of the second, where evidence shows it is general, is His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿O Prophet, when you divorce women, divorce them at their waiting period﴾ [al-Talaq 1]. His saying ﴿when you divorce﴾ is an address to a plural group, not to a single person, namely the Ummah. Yet He addressed their leader and their Messenger, because they follow him. So He said: ﴿O Prophet, when you divorce﴾. Therefore the address includes the Prophet ﷺ and the entire Ummah.

An example of what may bear both meanings is this verse: ﴿And recite what has been revealed to you of the Book of your Lord﴾. Someone may say that there is an indication in it that it is specific to him, as we will mention, Allah willing. However, examples of this are numerous, and the correct view is that the address is to the Ummah, but it is directed to its leader and exemplar, because important addresses are only directed to leaders and those who are followed.

His saying: ﴿what has been revealed to you of the Book of your Lord﴾ refers to the Qur'an. The attribution of "Lord" to the Messenger ﷺ is evidence that what Allah revealed to His Messenger is part of His complete care for him. ﴿None can alter His words﴾ means: no one is able to alter His words, neither the cosmic (kawniyya) words nor the legislative (shar'iyya) words. As for the cosmic words, it is obvious: no one can alter them. So when Allah, Exalted is He, says "Be" concerning a cosmic matter, no one can change it. Is that clear?

* Student: No one can alter the cosmic words of Allah, Mighty and Majestic is He.

* Shaykh: As for the cosmic words, no one is able to. As for the legislative words, no one is able to do so legally. So the negation here is not a negation of existence, but a negation of legal possibility: no one is able to alter Allah's legislative words in a lawful manner, never. Rather, it is obligatory upon everyone to submit to Allah, Mighty and Majestic.

If someone says: We have found people who alter the words of Allah. Has Allah not pointed to this in His saying about the Bedouins: ﴿They wish to change the words of Allah﴾ [al-Fath 15]?

We say: Yes, but this alteration is legislative, and legislative alteration may occur among humans, who distort words from their proper places and interpret the words of Allah with what Allah did not intend. Among this are all the negators (al-mu'attila) of the attributes of Allah, Mighty and Majestic, or some of them, from those who have altered the words of Allah.

﴿And you will not find besides Him any refuge﴾ means: you, O Messenger, will not find, apart from Allah, Mighty and Majestic, ﴿any refuge﴾, meaning anyone you can incline toward and seek shelter with. The root of "iltihad" is "lahd," which means inclination. In other words, if anyone intended harm to you, you would not find anyone to protect you apart from Allah, Mighty and Majestic. So when a person is afflicted by something harmful or feared, to whom does he seek refuge? To Allah, Mighty and Majestic. A parallel to this verse is His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Say, "Indeed, I do not possess for you any harm or right guidance." Say, "Indeed, no one will protect me from Allah, and I will not find besides Him any refuge."﴾ [al-Jinn 21-22].

Commentary of Ibn 'Uthaymin (Tafsir al-Quran al-Karim) on surah 18, verse 28:

﴿And restrain yourself to be with those who call upon their Lord morning and evening, seeking His Face﴾ [al-Kahf: 28] to the end of the verse. ﴿Restrain yourself﴾ means: keep yourself with those who call upon Allah, both in asking (du'a' al-mas'alah) and in worship (du'a' al-'ibadah). ﴿Morning﴾ means the beginning of the day, and ﴿evening﴾ means the end of the day, sincerely for Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, ﴿seeking His Face﴾, and not seeking anything of the worldly life. That is, they do this for Allah alone, not for anyone other than Him.

In the verse is the affirmation of the Face for Allah, the Mighty and Majestic. The scholars of Ahl al-Sunnah (the People of the Sunnah) have agreed on the establishment of the Face for Allah, the Exalted, due to the indication of the Book and the Sunnah regarding that. Allah, the Exalted, said: ﴿And there remains the Face of your Lord, Owner of Majesty and Honor﴾ [al-Rahman: 27], and the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "I seek refuge in Your Face" [Agreed upon; al-Bukhari (6227) and Muslim (2841/28) from the hadith of Abu Hurayrah]. The predecessors of the Ummah and its imams have also agreed on the establishment of the Face for Allah.

But would this Face be similar to the faces of created beings? Listen, my brothers, especially the newcomers: it is impossible for the Face of Allah to be similar to the faces of created beings, due to the saying of Allah, the Exalted: ﴿There is nothing like unto Him, and He is the All-Hearing, the All-Seeing﴾ [al-Shura: 11], and His saying, the Exalted: ﴿Lord of the heavens and the earth and whatever is between them, so worship Him and be steadfast in His worship. Do you know of any similar (samiyyan) to Him?﴾ [Maryam: 65], meaning: an equal or a counterpart. Allah, Blessed and Exalted, also said: ﴿So do not set up rivals to Allah while you know﴾ [al-Baqarah: 22]. Likewise, whatever Allah has described Himself with, it is obligatory upon us to take it according to its apparent meaning, but without tamthil (likening).

If someone says: "If you affirm for Allah a face, it necessarily entails likening, and so we interpret His saying: ﴿There is nothing like unto Him﴾ as meaning: except in what He has affirmed, such as the face and the two hands, for example?"

The answer: This is obstinacy, because we know by the senses and by reason that everything attributed to a thing corresponds to that thing. Does a human not have a face, a camel have a face, a horse have a face, and an elephant have a face? Are these faces alike? No, never; each suits what it is attributed to. Indeed, even time and periods have a face, as in the saying of Allah, the Exalted: ﴿Believe at the face of the day and reject at its end﴾ [Al 'Imran: 72]; ﴿the face of the day﴾ — so He affirmed a face for a period of time. Can anyone say that the face of the day is like the face of a human? It is not possible.

Therefore, what Allah has attributed to Himself of a face cannot be similar to the faces of created beings, because every attribute suits the one described.

If someone says: "There has come in the authentic hadith that the Prophet (ﷺ) said: 'Indeed Allah, the Exalted, created Adam upon His image (ṣūrah)' [Agreed upon; al-Bukhari (6227) and Muslim (2841/28) from the hadith of Abu Hurayrah]." So what is the answer?

The answer is from one of two aspects:

Either it is said: "upon His image," but it does not follow from being upon His image that it is like Him. The proof is that the Prophet (ﷺ) informed that "the first group to enter Paradise will be in the image of the moon on the night of the full moon" [Agreed upon; al-Bukhari (3245) and Muslim (2834/17) from the hadith of Abu Hurayrah], and we know there is no likeness between those people and the moon, but they are upon its image in general terms: in brightness, radiance and light.

The second aspect: it is said: "upon His image," meaning: upon the image which He chose, the Mighty and Majestic. The attribution of the human form to Allah is by way of honor and glorification, as in the saying of Allah, the Exalted: ﴿And who is more unjust than one who prevents the mosques of Allah from having His name mentioned therein﴾ [al-Baqarah: 114]. It is known that Allah does not pray in mosques, but they were attributed to Allah by way of what? Honor and glorification; and because they were built for the obedience of Allah. Likewise the saying of Salih to his people: ﴿The she-camel of Allah and her drinking﴾ [al-Shams: 13]. It is known that this she-camel is not something Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, rides; but it was attributed to Allah by way of honor and glorification. So the creation of Adam upon His image, or upon the image of the Most Merciful, means: upon the form which He chose from among all other creatures.

Allah, the Exalted, said in Surat al-Infitar: ﴿O mankind, what has deceived you concerning your Lord, the Generous? (6) Who created you, then proportioned you, then made you balanced﴾ [al-Infitar: 6-7], meaning: He made you of balanced proportion, and this includes the balance of stature and the balance of form.

So we have now understood, praise be to Allah, that Allah, the Exalted, has a real Face and that it does not resemble the faces of created beings.

﴿Seeking His Face﴾: in this is an indication of sincerity (ikhlas), from His saying: ﴿seeking His Face﴾. So, my Muslim brother, hold to sincerity so that you benefit from the deed.

﴿And let not your eyes pass beyond them, desiring adornment of the worldly life﴾: that is, do not let your eyes turn away from these noble masters. ﴿Desiring adornment of the worldly life﴾ — rather, make your gaze toward them constant and your companionship with them constant. In His saying: ﴿desiring adornment of the worldly life﴾ is an indication that if the Messenger (ﷺ) parted from them for a religious benefit, would this fall under the prohibition or not? No; the prohibition is to leave the people of goodness for the sake of the world, not for a religious benefit.

﴿And do not obey one whose heart We have made heedless of Our remembrance and who follows his desire and whose affair has been [ever] in neglect﴾ [al-Kahf: 28]. ﴿Do not obey one whose heart We have made heedless of Our remembrance﴾ means: of His mentioning us, or of the reminder which We sent down. According to the first, the meaning is that a person who mentions Allah with his tongue but not his heart is included in the verse; according to the second, the meaning is the man whom Allah has made heedless of the Qur'an, so that he pays it no heed and sees no harm in opposing it.

﴿And do not obey one whose heart We have made heedless of Our remembrance and who follows his desire﴾ and does not follow guidance; ﴿and whose affair﴾ means: his state; ﴿has been [ever] in neglect﴾ means: squandered, the days and nights passing while he feels nothing.

* In this verse is an indication of the importance of presence of heart when remembering Allah, and that the person who mentions Allah with his tongue but not his heart has blessing removed from his deeds and his times, so that his affair becomes neglect (furuṭan) for him. You find him spending long hours and having achieved nothing; but if his heart were with Allah, blessing would be obtained for all his works. ﴿And whose affair has been [ever] in neglect﴾.

Then He, Mighty and Majestic, says: ﴿And say: The truth is from your Lord﴾ [Al-Kahf 29]. ﴿Say﴾: to whom is the address? To the Messenger ﷺ; that is, say it openly. ﴿The truth is from your Lord﴾, not from anyone else.
